stories.title: No surge in bookings but eclipse 'boosts footfall'
stories.summary: Tourism chiefs say region can benefit from events like the partial solar eclipse.
stories.post: 📰 NEWS: No surge in bookings but eclipse 'boosts footfall'. Tourism chiefs say region can benefit from events like the partial solar eclipse. Source: BBC Science.
article_sentences: With the partial eclipse taking place on Wednesday evening, large crowds are expected to gather in many areas in the South West and Channel Islands.
In Devon and Cornwall, the entire event is set to last about one hour and 50 minutes, starting at about 18:20 BST and finishing by 20:10.

Tourism leaders say they have not seen "a significant surge" in tourism or last-minute hotel bookings triggered by the eclipse but people attracted by the spectacle may have secured accommodation in advance.
Sarah Gibson, chief executive of Plymouth Waterfront Partnership said the combination of the eclipse and the British Fireworks Championships in the city was sure to boost footfall in the city.
General manager of Visit Devon Sally Everton said "astrotourism is an important and growing opportunity for Devon".
She added: "I have spoken with several local businesses and, so far, we have not seen a significant surge in tourism or additional hotel bookings specifically linked to the eclipse.
"We have seen increased footfall this year, although visitor spend appears to be lower.
It may be that many dedicated eclipse and stargazing visitors have already arrived and planned their trips well in advance."

There are a range of free and ticketed events being held in Devon and Cornwall to help people enjoy the spectacle, with venues including a spectacular beachside spot, an observatory and even a pub with its own observatory.
Everton said: "What we are hearing locally is that many local people are planning to head to key viewing locations to experience the eclipse."
She said the eclipse emphasised the huge opportunities for astrotourism in the region.
"We have excellent stargazing locations, most notably Exmoor National Park, an International Dark Sky Reserve, alongside the protected landscapes of Dartmoor and other rural areas.
